confidence_note: The DB lists the book as 'Sağlıklı Olmak' by James Clear (2019); no such book exists. The story comes from Atomic Habits (2018), chapter 1, verified on Clear's own site. Clear later corrected the 2008 share to 8 of 14 road and track golds (57%), and added an update that the team's use of therapeutic use exemptions was questioned and investigations were unresolved; this goes in as a caveat. Old 'one more glass of water' example is not the book's. Medium because of the title mismatch.
facts: In 2003 British Cycling hired Dave Brailsford as performance director. British riders had won one Olympic gold since 1908, no Briton had won the Tour de France in 110 years, and a top European bike maker refused to sell to the team for fear of hurting its sales.
Brailsford's plan: the aggregation of marginal gains, finding a 1% improvement in everything the team did.

Gains included redesigned bike seats, alcohol rubbed on tires for grip, testing massage gels, the best pillow and mattress for each rider, a surgeon teaching riders to wash their hands to catch fewer colds, and the inside of the team truck painted white to spot dust.

At the 2008 Beijing Olympics the team won 8 of 14 road and track golds; in 2012 Bradley Wiggins became the first British Tour de France winner. From 2007 to 2017 British riders won 178 world championships, 66 Olympic or Paralympic golds and 5 Tours de France.
Clear's arithmetic: 1% better every day for a year is about 37 times better; 1% worse every day ends near zero.
Clear: every action is a vote for the type of person you wish to become.

Caveat: Clear later posted an update that questions had been raised about the team's use of therapeutic use exemptions and that investigations were unresolved; he says the chapter is about compounding habits, not cycling.

tension: A national team with one Olympic gold in a century started by fixing pillows and hand washing.
opening_idea: Start with a surgeon teaching professional cyclists how to wash their hands.

lessons.idea: Look for the small health inputs you repeat every day, such as sleep, hygiene and the first drink of the day, because they compound.
lessons.anchor: pillows, mattresses and hand washing in a cycling team

reflect_final: Which daily health detail, like your pillow, your water or the way you wash your hands, have you never thought worth improving by one percent?

use_cases.situation: Family wants to 'get healthy' all at once
use_cases.move: Pick one daily detail like bedtime or water; adjust it this week.

use_cases.situation: Team planning a big wellness program
use_cases.move: Mention British Cycling started with hand washing and pillows; start with one small daily thing.

use_cases.situation: You fall off an ambitious diet
use_cases.move: Ask what a 1% better version of today's meal looks like.

pocket_idea: A world-beating team started with pillows and hand washing; improve one daily health detail by a little.
